articles.title_orig: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be the hardest to stop
articles.title_zh: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be the hardest to stop
articles.content_orig:
It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.
But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."
It's not just a threat to jobs . They warn that  allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.
One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.
And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.
"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.
Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks , which could be accelerated by capable AI.
"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."
The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.
At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.
AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems , doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture .
We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.
It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.
To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.
But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.
But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.
Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.
Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.
The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until  the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?
With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.
"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.
"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"
It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military , for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.
If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle , its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.
"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.
States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?
"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.
Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.
If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.
"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.
"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."
Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.

articles.title_orig: Unprecedented Collab Between China and the Met Uncovers Secrets of Chinese Mural During Exhaustive Reproduction
articles.title_zh: Unprecedented Collab Between China and the Met Uncovers Secrets of Chinese Mural During Exhaustive Reproduction
articles.content_orig:
A major arts and heritage conservation project in China has born unexpected fruit thousands of miles away in New York City.
In the Chinese arts and antiquities gallery of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a 50-foot-long mural devours the attention of an entire room with its arrangement of Buddha and his attendants.
The Medicine Buddha mural had long attracted the wonder of Zhang Jian, director of the “Meticulous Painting Institute” at the Chinese National Academy of Arts, which since 2013 has poured billions of Chinese RMB into restoring, conserving, and repatriating Chinese artifacts around the country and the world.
Describing it as wielding an “awe-inspiring energy,” Zhang learned that the mural was originally located in the ancient Guangsheng Temple in central China. Standing in its halls years later, staring at the vacant space where the massive mural had originally hung, Zhang was struck with an idea.
Over the next 3 years, he led a team of special artists and conservationists to the Met to meticulously—excruciatingly—copy the mural for a life-sized replica that captures every single crack, faded contour, and conservationist correction it had faced in its 700 years on the Earth.
This project was made possible with the unerring support of the Met itself, a collaboration which marks arguably the highest ever undertaken between Chinese and American cultural institutes.
Now in October, the Met is to co-host an international symposium in Beijing about Chinese murals, marking the first time the New York museum has jointly held a major academic conference in China with a national research body.
Jason Sun, the Met’s curator of Chinese art, told the South China Morning Post that the results achieved by Zhang’s team—including the realization that conservators had incorrectly arranged the mural segments so that Lord Buddha’s head was 2 centimeters off kilter—as having “profound historical and practical significance.”
Painted around 700 years ago during the Mongol-administered Yuan Dynasty, on clay tiles mixed with rice straw, the mural depicts the Medicine Buddha seated with his chief attendants surrounded by numerous figures.
Yet its presence in the Met isn’t the result of it being a plundered relic. Mainland China was mostly free from Western colonial occupation when the impoverished monks from Guangsheng Temple chopped the mural up into sections and sold it to fix the collapsing roof of their temple.
Among the keystones of Buddha’s teachings is the unavoidable truth that all things are impermanent, so if they were good students of the Great Sage, those impoverished monks would not have hesitated to part with the relic, that traded hands across the West until it arrived at the Met via donation from Arthur Sackler in 1965.
The China National Arts Fund, a state-endowed philanthropic fund established in 2013 under the National Academy of Arts, was as recently as 2025 tasked specifically with the preservation of ancient murals and other works. So far, 40 ancient murals from caves and temples across Western China have been painstakingly examined and copied, but if they are held overseas, the Fund has the directive to pay for their study, and potentially, their recreation.
Yet Zhang had a different sort of intention for that recreation: one that the Met administrators enthusiastically supported. In 2024, SCMP reports that the Fund had formalized a research partnership with the Met, whereby the famous museum granted their colleagues in East Asia full authorization for prolonged detailed study of the work, and the sharing of ultra-high-resolution digital images.
CHINESE MURALS IN THE NEWS: Stunning Tang Dynasty Mural Unearthed in China Portrays a ‘Westerner’ with Blonde Hair
“The Met staff actively coordinated with visitors for us,” said Meng Ying, an artist on Zhang’s team which visited the Met 3 times over the following years. “Though our lifts and lighting equipment occasionally blocked sightlines, visitors were remarkably understanding.”
As Meng said, studying portions of the work required specialized hydraulic lifts and expansive light fixtures, conditions which he described as being “unprecedented” in the history of the Met. This went on for days at a time, while the team poured their attention onto the smallest details to reproduce exactly what it was that the Guangsheng Temple was missing.
This included using clay-rich mud and rice straw to make the tiles, which they sourced from as close to the temple as possible. It involved extensive studying into the mineral pigments—considering what would have been available to the medieval painters, and how such materials could have changed over 700 years.
“Lighting, digital cameras ,and printing all change how a color looks. We had to tweak our paints over and over again on site,” said Han Maoyuan, another artist on the team.
MORE COLLABORATION LIKE THIS: Since 1968 French Teachers Have Come to Louisiana Classrooms to Preserve French Language Through Immersion
Yet further, the team layered their mud tiles to create a base-layer painting and a second to replicate the scars left by time and intervention.
As mentioned earlier, the team’s exhaustive examination of the mural revealed that its original mounters in the Met’s galleries had misunderstood Chinese brushwork, and misaligned the Buddha’s head by 2 centimeters. Met staff told SCMP that after the disbelief wore off, they couldn’t walk through the room without noticing that the Buddha’s head was crooked.
The finished mural produced by Zhang and his team made its public debut at the China National Arts and Crafts Museum in Beijing, where on September 24th, in honor of President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US, an exhibition was held featuring the fruits of the National Art Fund’s preservation and reproduction efforts.
FROM THE MET: Rare Chinese ‘Magic Mirror’ That Projects Hidden Image Rediscovered After Decades in Museum Storage
Zhang said it would allow this ancient mural to re-enter contemporary cultural life, yet with all the context that great works of art carry with them as the centuries load up on their shoulders.
Other murals from Guangsheng, as it turns out, are located in American Museums—in Cincinnati and Missouri—both have which have already contacted Zhang for the purpose of examining the alignments and conditions of the works.

articles.title_orig: Finland gripped by national broadcaster’s puppies live stream
articles.title_zh: Finland gripped by national broadcaster’s puppies live stream
articles.content_orig:
It’s dark outside. The news cycle is relentless. But Finland ’s national broadcaster has a solution: Adorable puppies , available any time, night or day.
Yle has been drawing millions of people to its website with “ Pentulive ” – Finnish for “Puppy Live” – a 24/7 live stream of Hilkka, a Lagotto Romagnolo dog, and her brand-new litter of puppies as they sleep, play and suckle enthusiastically.
Hilkka gave birth to the two females and four males on October 10. The webcam was switched on shortly after, and the puppies will remain in the spotlight until they leave for their new homes in December.
Given that puppies need up to 20 hours of sleep a day, the action can be limited, which may explain why “Pentulive,” now in its sixth season, has been labelled “ slow TV ” – a concept first trialed in Norway in 2009 with the Norwegian public broadcaster’s airing of a seven-hour train journey.
Nonetheless, viewers who tune in to the home of the anonymous breeder have been promised the chance to witness some of the “puppies’ milestone moments,” according to a Yle press statement: from opening their eyes to learning to walk and having their first playtime outside.
Despite Finland’s tiny population – just under 5.66 million – the “Pentulive” webpage had 6.5 million page views last year, according to Yle, and its social media channels attracted 20 million views. And based on viewing figures so far, this year’s puppies look set to outperform.
One of the world’s northernmost countries, Finland is preparing to usher in its long, dark winter. Temperatures can drop as low as -50°C (-58°F) and in parts of the country north of the Arctic Circle the sun does not rise above the horizon for weeks on end.
So it is hardly surprising that residents enjoy a cozy distraction from the bitter conditions outside.
How a 24-hour livestream of moose became a Swedish TV sensation
The puppy-cam was first launched in 2021 by Yle science reporter Pirjo Koskinen as part of a series on canine science. She told CNN in an email that the idea was, in part, “to shed light on a dog’s crucial first few weeks,” adding: “What happens at the breeder’s – much like with human children – influences the rest of the dog’s life.”
Distraction from the harsh reality of daily life is part of “Pentulive“‘s appeal, Koskinen believes. “It is all about caring, love, and nurturing – all those positive aspects of humanity that often get pushed aside by a constant stream of unpleasant news,” she said.
“‘Puppy Live’ offers comfort and relaxation amidst the rush of everyday life; it’s a wonderful escape from the human world into a ‘puppy bubble.’”
Sonja Mutanen, a doctoral researcher studying media and animals at the University of Eastern Finland, explained its particular appeal to Finns.
“For many viewers, these live streams are a much-anticipated highlight of the dark Finnish winter months,” she told CNN. “This kind of feel-good content can foster a sense of belonging and emotional well-being, which is important during late autumn and winter when people tend to stay at home more.”
Miiamaaria Kujala, adjunct professor of comparative cognitive neuroscience at the University of Helsinki, said in an email to CNN that a live feed affects us in a completely different way from the short reels that are now commonplace on social media.
“The live stream offers something that appears to be missing from many of the modern busy lives: something real, genuine and fragile,” she said. “Pentulive is life-paced: It contains very calm periods and unexpectable action periods. As a live feed, it likely provokes more intense emotional responses from the observers … but it is also immensely calming to observe a sleeping puppy.”
It also provides a “sense of continuity as it follows the puppies growing older,” she said, adding: “They’re not just random animals, you learn to know them individually.”
Puppies are born ready to interact with people, study finds
This is the second litter for 5-year-old Hilkka, who is currently on leave from her role as a “school dog,” where she provides emotional support for pupils.
So far, the fluffballs have only been given nicknames by their breeder, but on Saturday they will be officially renamed. The viewing public will narrow down a selection of names, from which the puppies themselves will “choose” – by sitting in a circle of sealed envelopes and snuffling at the one that appeals.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts,’ and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia executes 2 Bangladeshis over ‘indecent acts,’ and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.
A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.
According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.
The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.
Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive / Saudi postpones FII in person after Wall Street lobbying
articles.title_zh: Exclusive / Saudi postpones FII in person after Wall Street lobbying
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia has canceled in-person attendance at its flagship investment conference in Riyadh after Wall Street executives privately relayed safety concerns to organizers, including the boss of the kingdomâs sovereign wealth fund, people familiar with the matter said. Organizers of the Future Investment Initiative, due to take place next week, have dropped plans for a gathering of global and regional chief executives, and are telling delegates the event is postponed until 2027, the people said, confirming a Semafor story that a decision to postpone would be made today. The conference, which has become informally known as âDavos in the Desert,â is Saudi Arabiaâs highest profile event, attended by some of the biggest names in global finance and business. Next weekâs edition had been set to host JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon, Goldman Sachs CEO David Solomon, and BlackRock CEO Larry Fink. Big banks and private equity firms had been privately relaying safety concerns about attending FII to Yasir Al-Rumayyan, Semafor reported earlier, according to people familiar with the matter.
Multiple signals suggested FII could be postponed: Rooms at the Ritz Carlton in Riyadh, which is usually blocked for the event, have been available for public booking in the past 24 hours. Other scheduled events such as an exhibition tennis tournament, a charity event linked to the crown prince, and Riyadh Fashion Week have all been postponed after the Houthis escalated attacks on the kingdom.
Delaying the conference is not surprising as the airport appears to still be closed, the main business district has instructed tenants to work from home until further notice, and schools have also shifted to home learning.
The kingdom, and its neighbors like the UAE and Qatar, have pitched themselves as not just sources of capital, but as a safe home for trillions in financial assets, data centers, and new industries.
Speculation has swirled in recent weeks over whether Saudi Arabia would go forward with the event, given high-profile attacks on the Riyadh airport. Organizers have held discussions around allowing overseas executives to participate virtually , Reuters reported last week, and The Wall Street Journal said that some executives had already canceled meetings .
The US, along with most other Western governments, recommends against all but essential travel to Saudi Arabia. That has knock-on effects on travel insurance costs and advice from internal security and risk teams.
Still, Saudi Arabia has viewed attendance at the event, and general support for the Gulf during turbulent times, as a loyalty test for global business leaders. Those who show up in tough times are rewarded, while fair-weather friends are often excluded from lucrative deals .
This story has been updated to reflect FIIâs decision to cancel the in-person meeting.

articles.title_orig: 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
articles.title_zh: 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
articles.content_orig:
Metro workers repair tracks damaged in a Russian attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 19, 2026. (Chris Occhicone/The Kyiv Independent)
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
At least one person was killed and eight others injured after multiple waves of Russian missiles struck Kyiv overnight on Oct. 19.
Several explosions rocked the capital just before 11 p.m., with further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m., Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported. Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said damage was reported in at least three districts.
One person was killed in the Desnianskyi District where a non-residential building caught fire and a metro station was damaged, DSNS said. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko earlier reported a fatality was that of 21-year-old woman.
The above-ground Chernihivska and Lisova metro stations were temporarily closed for repairs, city officials said.
Later on Oct. 19, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said more than 70 workers were repairing the damaged metro infrastructure, with the most difficult work involving power supply and train control systems. Repairs had continued since overnight but were being slowed by air raid alerts, which forced crews to take shelter.
Train service between Lisova and Akademmistechko stations was expected to resume that evening, with trains skipping Chernihivska until repairs were completed, Klitschko added.
Five people were injured in the Solomianskyi District when a 25-story residential building was damaged, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. It is not yet clear where the other injuries occurred.
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
The Cosmo Multimall shopping and entertainment center sustained significant damage in the Solomianskyi District. Its administration said no employees were injured and that the mall was working to resume operations as soon as possible. The center did not disclose the extent of the damage or provide a timeline for repairs.
Serhii Misan, 68, a local resident, had planned to pick up his new refrigerator from Cosmo Multimall on the morning of Oct. 19.
"I only paid for a refrigerator yesterday, and they told me I could pick it up today," Misan said. "And now look at what's happening here."
"(The Russians) are terrorists. They strike civilian targets. They spare no one — not children, not equipment, no one. They just kill civilians."
Misan added that, in light of recent developments, Ukraine would struggle to resist Russia without a strong partner like the U.S.
"If aid is reduced, it will be very difficult to stand up to an aggressor like Russia," he said. "We are not trying to seize their land. We are trying to defend our right to live freely on our own land."
Sofiia Kelli, 18, who lives in the Solomianskyi district, told The Kyiv Independent that her apartment was also damaged in the Russian attack on the capital. Her family was only able to take shelter in an underground parking garage after the attack began, as there was too little time between the air raid alert and the strikes.
"It was a huge shock. It was extremely loud — nothing like the other explosions we've heard in our neighborhood," Kelli said.
"I couldn't fall asleep afterward. Then I just sat in the bathroom and cried for a very long time. It's hard to process everything that happened because you always think something like this won't happen to you. And then it does."
"They [Russians] strike civilian targets. They [Russians] spare no one — not children, not equipment, no one. They [Russians] just kill civilians."
Kelli said she intends to stay in Kyiv despite the latest attack and is getting ready for the coming winter.
"Everything depends on electricity. Of course, it's difficult, but we're doing the best we can. We've installed solar panels (on the building) and a generator to keep the elevators running," she added.
Klitschko also reported damage to a medical center in the same district. The blast wave shattered more than 200 windows, damaged doors and ceilings, and damaged medical equipment, he said.
No medical center staff were injured, and there were no patients inside the facility at the time of the attack.
The Russian attack also destroyed a data center operated by telecommunications company Datagroup, which provides electronic communications services to users in more than 90 settlements across Ukraine.
The company said the facility's equipment and infrastructure had been damaged beyond repair. No employees were injured in the attack.
Russian attacks also hit settlements in Kyiv Oblast surrounding the capital. In Irpin, about 20 kilometers (12 miles) northwest of Kyiv, one woman was killed and 19 people were injured, including nine children.
At around 9 a.m. local time, Tymur Tkachenko , head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said that three people were missing. Search operations are ongoing, he added.
The Russian strikes damaged 70 houses, five apartment buildings, industrial facilities, and warehouses in Irpin, according to Tkachenko.
Recent ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv have arrived with little or no advance warning amid deteriorating relations between Ukraine and the U.S., which provides intelligence used to track Russian missile launches.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on the morning of Oct. 19 that Russian forces had attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles, adding that Kyiv had received no advance warning from its partners about the launches.
According to Zelensky, Russia fired 16 ballistic missiles, with Kyiv and the surrounding region being the primary targets.
"When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defense are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners," Zelensky wrote on X.
"The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia's desire to drag this war out."
Yurii Ihnat, head of the Ukrainian Air Force's communications department, said on national television that Russia launched two waves of ballistic missile attacks overnight on Oct. 19, at around 11 p.m. and 3 a.m. local time.
Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners ahead of the first wave, but information about the second wave was provided, Ihnat said.
He added that a similar situation had occurred during previous attacks, including the one overnight on Oct. 14.
"Information was indeed not provided the first time, for certain reasons. Our experts are looking into this together with our partners, as this is not the first time such a situation has occurred. Information was provided at 3 a.m.," Ihnat said.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened."
Commenting on Ukrainian officials' claims that partners had not provided advance warning of Russia's ballistic missile launches overnight, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on the morning of Oct. 19 that he "did not know exactly" what had happened.
"I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving (Ukrainian) early warning system," Rubio said.
"I know that EUCOM (U.S. European Command) had been involved in looking at, and that's the report they gave us back.  I can't comment on what happened last night," he added.

Alerts did sound before the overnight strikes though the warnings were unusually short. The first explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Phone alerts went off moments before the blasts, while the street sirens began "howling during the explosions," Chief Editor Olga Rudenko reported.

articles.title_orig: Micron, Intel lead chip recovery, adding nearly $250B as most of Wall Street falls: Chart of the Day
articles.title_zh: Micron, Intel lead chip recovery, adding nearly $250B as most of Wall Street falls: Chart of the Day
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Last week, chip stocks helped drag Wall Street lower. Monday, they're lifting the indexes while most stocks keep falling.
A Yahoo Finance basket of 60 chip-related stocks is recovering nearly $250 billion in market value, with gains reaching across memory makers, chip designers, and equipment suppliers.
Micron ( MU ) and Intel ( INTC ) are each gaining over 2%, while Sandisk ( SNDK ) is up nearly 5%. AMD ( AMD ), Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Western Digital ( WDC ) are joining the rebound.
Nearly 90% of the stocks in the chip basket are higher. Across the S&P 500, roughly 70% are falling, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
The equal-weight S&P 500 ETF ( RSP ) is lower even as the main index advances, showing how much the headline recovery depends on a relatively small group of winners.
Many of those buyers are returning to familiar territory.
Micron and Sandisk lost roughly 15% and 18%, respectively, last week, as memory stocks entered another bear market . Both helped power the spring rally from the March lows as hopes of a US-Iran ceasefire improved.
That earlier leadership is showing up beyond individual chip names. Among the S&P 500's 100 strongest performers from March 30 through June 2 — the first big leg higher after war headlines faded — 61 are rising Monday. Among the 100 weakest, 84 are falling.
Intel also has a fresh catalyst. JPMorgan upgraded it to Neutral from Underweight, citing opportunities tied to AI demand and chip scarcity, as Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports .
The rebound is getting a tougher reception elsewhere in AI.
CoreWeave ( CRWV ) has surrendered most of its premarket gains despite a Goldman Sachs upgrade to Buy . The cloud provider's financing needs were front and center in last week's selling.
Semiconductor stocks have also pulled back since the open. For chip bulls, the PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) would ideally close above 11,500 today and needs to hold the 11,000-11,100 area to avoid a larger washout.

articles.title_orig: Wyze’s latest weight scale has a display you can actually see, Google Health sync
articles.title_zh: Wyze’s latest weight scale has a display you can actually see, Google Health sync
articles.content_orig:
Wyze has released a new BodyScan Plus scale that syncs with Google Health and Android Health Connect while fixing a long-running problem with scales – this one actually lets you see the display.
Available starting today as a part of “Wyze Week,” the Wyze Scale Ultra BodyScan Plus continues its mouthful of a name, but with some nice features to back it up.
The Wyze Scale Ultra Bodyscan launched in late 2025 with this new Plus model being its sequel. It’s a bit more expensive at $149 – what isn’t more expensive in 2026 – and makes one key hardware change. Where the original made itself stand out by putting sensors on a bar that you could raise up to get more details on muscle mass and more, it still put the display at your feet, making it a bit harder to see those results.
Wyze Scale Ultra Bodyscan Plus moves the display over to that bar, letting you see everything way closer to eye level.
When just tracking weight without the added sensors, the display is still at your feet, but the bar lets you lift that up for easier readability.
That’s on top of the scale supporting the same metrics including “weight, BMI, body fat percentage, muscle mass, body water, visceral fat, protein, bone mass, basal metabolic rate,” and others. The scale requires no subscription, nor does it even require a Bluetooth connection to your phone. Built-in Wi-Fi means it can sync with the Wyze app on its own while also being able to connect into Google Health and Apple Health, as well as leverage Android’s Health Connect to tie into other apps.
Wyze Scale Ultra Bodyscan Plus is available today for $149.
Wyze also has a more affordable scale with similar tracking that costs around $80.

articles.title_orig: New nonstop Lufthansa flight announced from Columbus to Frankfurt
articles.title_zh: New nonstop Lufthansa flight announced from Columbus to Frankfurt
articles.content_orig:
Published: October 19, 2026
(COLUMBUS) The Columbus Regional Airport Authority, Lufthansa Airlines, JobsOhio and One Columbus today announced that Central Ohio's first nonstop flight to Europe will launch in May 2027, connecting John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) with Frankfurt Airport (FRA) in Germany. The new service marks a major milestone for the Columbus Region and Ohio, providing direct access to one of the world's leading international hubs and creating new opportunities for businesses, travelers and visitors throughout the state.
“Today's announcement is a tremendous milestone for the Columbus Region and Ohio,” said Daren Griffin, CRAA President and CEO. “Lufthansa's new nonstop service to Frankfurt provides our passengers with a direct link to one of the world's strongest global networks, enhancing connectivity, competitiveness and continued growth. We are grateful to Lufthansa, JobsOhio, One Columbus, our business community and so many others whose partnership helped make this opportunity possible. At a time of extraordinary transformation for our airports and our region, this new service establishes Ohio's gateway to continental Europe. It strengthens our state's connections to the global economy and creates new opportunities for communities across Ohio. We couldn't be more excited about what it means for our businesses, travelers and the future of Ohio”
This will be Ohio's first and only nonstop flight to Germany, serving hundreds of daily passengers from Columbus and across Ohio who travel to Europe each day. Lufthansa will operate the service with a Boeing 787 Dreamliner featuring the airline's Allegris cabin experience, including 28 lie-flat business class seats, 28 premium economy seats and 231 economy seats, for a total of 287 seats.
“We are very pleased to connect Columbus and the state of Ohio directly with our Frankfurt hub, the first intercontinental flight from this great city,” said Dirk Janzen, Lufthansa Group Vice President of Passenger Sales, the Americas. “The new service will provide both business and leisure travelers with a convenient nonstop connection to Germany, as well as onward destinations across our Lufthansa Group network. The launch of this route is an important step in our continued expansion in the United States, our most important market outside the Lufthansa Group’s home markets. We look forward to strengthening the connections between Ohio and Europe, and to welcoming travelers from Columbus and the surrounding region,” Janzen added.
The flight will provide unprecedented connectivity for the 38 German-based companies operating in the Columbus Region and further support all German companies investing in Ohio and employing thousands of Ohioans across the state. Through Lufthansa's Frankfurt hub, travelers will have convenient access to more than 130 destinations across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and India.
The new service is also expected to make it easier for international visitors, investors and talent to access the Columbus Region and explore opportunities across Ohio, further supporting the state's economic development efforts.
“Ohio is committed to building a collaborative partnership with Lufthansa to support the success of this new route and strengthen the significant ties that benefit both of our regions,” said Ohio Governor Mike DeWine. “This new route will be transformative, giving our state access to critical markets in Germany, Europe and the world while establishing stronger economic, research, cultural and educational exchanges.”
Germany is the third-largest source of international investment in Ohio, behind only Japan and Canada. More than 750 German-owned business establishments operate in Ohio, second only to Japan, according to the Ohio Department of Development, and German companies support approximately 41,000 jobs across the state, according to the Transatlantic Economy 2025 report. Ohio businesses also exported nearly $1.4 billion in goods to Germany in 2023. Overall, Ohio ranks third in the nation for foreign direct investment, with about 4,000 companies from 42 countries operating in the state.
The new route builds on the success of JobsOhio’s Air Service Restoration program, which works with airports, regional partners and airlines to establish routes that are important to economic development. JobsOhio created the program after businesses and stakeholders said during a 2019 statewide listening tour that air service at Ohio airports had declined more sharply than in competitor states. Through the program, JobsOhio and regional partners share revenue guarantees that reduce the risk for airlines launching new service.
Since 2020, it has helped bring 32 new routes and 15 route expansions with six airlines to five Ohio airports, adding more than 590,000 new seats and more than 187,000 additional seats each year and generating an estimated $230 million in annual economic impact. JobsOhio has committed $36.8 million in revenue guarantees, alongside $10.1 million from local partners.
“Businesses, including the German companies that employ tens of thousands of Ohioans, tell us that better air service is essential to investing and creating jobs in Ohio,” said JobsOhio President and CEO J.P. Nauseef. “We listened, and this direct link to Frankfurt is exactly what our Air Service Restoration program was built to deliver.”
The new air service comes as the Columbus Region experiences some of the strongest economic growth in the country. The Columbus metro leads the Midwest in job creation, adding nearly 12,000 jobs between March 2025 and March 2026, with a growth rate more than 18 times the national average. The Region’s population also grew by more than 21,000 residents in 2025, twice the national growth rate. The new international connection is expected to further strengthen the Region’s ability to attract businesses, investment and talent from around the world.
“The Columbus Region is in the middle of an extraordinary stretch of job creation and business investment, and now we’re adding direct access to one of Europe’s most important business hubs,” said Jonas Peterson, Chief Economic Development Officer and President of One Columbus. “That’s a significant competitive advantage. It makes it easier for global companies to invest here, strengthens connections for businesses already operating in our Region and improves our ability to compete for the next major project. We have tremendous economic momentum right now, and this new connection gives us an opportunity to accelerate it even further.”
The Columbus Region continues to attract global investment and advanced industries, including recent commitments from companies such as Anduril, Intel and Bayer. The new Lufthansa service further strengthens Ohio's position as a destination for business growth and international commerce.
The CMH-FRA route will begin operating in May 2027, with bookings available beginning Tuesday, Oct. 20. Service will operate three times weekly on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays. Flights will depart Columbus at 4:20 p.m. and arrive in Frankfurt at 6:15 a.m. (local times).
The Lufthansa Group is a globally operating aviation group, with more than 100,000 employees worldwide. It is Europe's largest airline group by revenue, generating revenue of EUR 39.6 billion (EUR 39,597 million) in the 2025 financial year. The Lufthansa Group comprises mulitple business segments, including Passenger Airlines, Logistics, Technology (Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul), as well as other companies and group functions, including IT services and Lufthansa Aviation Training.
The Lufthansa Group’s portfolio of airlines includes Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, ITA Airways, Eurowings and Discover Airlines, connecting customers to destinations around the globe. articles.title_orig: Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov, 51, OBM
articles.title_zh: Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov, 51, OBM
articles.content_orig:
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a longtime educator and respected member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday morning. Full Story
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a longtime educator and respected member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday morning. Full Story
Rabbi Shmuel Yitzchak Malov , a beloved educator and longtime member of the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad, Kiryat Malachi, passed away suddenly on Monday, 8 Cheshvan, 5787.
Rabbi Malov suffered a sudden cardiac arrest shortly after waking up and washing Negel Vasser. Emergency responders were called to his home but were unable to revive him.
His sudden passing has shocked the Chabad community in Nachlas Har Chabad and his many friends and acquaintances throughout Israel and around the world.
Rabbi Malov served as the Rebbe’s Shliach in Kfar HaRif and dedicated much of his life to Jewish education. For many years, he directed the neighborhood’s evening yeshiva program, where hundreds of children gathered nightly in the local shul to study Torah.
Friends described him as a devoted educator and accomplished Torah scholar, knowledgeable in both Nigleh and Chassidus, who worked tirelessly to spread Torah learning.
He also organized annual Kinusei Torah in the neighborhood around Yom Tov, in accordance with the Rebbe’s directive to hold Torah gatherings during the holidays.
Rabbi Malov was the son-in-law of Rabbi Yitzchak Yehuda Yeruslavsky , Rov of Nachlas Har Chabad and a leading Chabad Rov.
He was born in Bnei Brak to Rabbi Tzvi Eliyahu Malov , OBM, a longtime Chabad communal activist in Yerushalayim who passed away approximately six years ago, and Mrs. Chana Chaya Malov , daughter of R’ Yaakov Moshe Hakohen Halperin , who passed away in Tishrei 5751 at the age of 40.
He is survived by his wife, Mrs. Nechama Dina Malov , and their children: Menachem Mendel, Shterna Sarah Kramer, Devorah Leah , and Mushka .
The levaya will depart from his home in Nachlas Har Chabad at 12:30 PM, passing the local Talmud Torah and central shul before proceeding to Shamgar in Yerushalayim.
The levaya will depart Shamgar at 3:00 PM for burial at Har Hamenuchos in Yerushalayim.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Home-Builder Sentiment Sinks to 14-Year Low
articles.title_zh: U.S. Home-Builder Sentiment Sinks to 14-Year Low
articles.content_orig:
The mood among America's homebuilders is grim.
Homebuilder sentiment fell three points to 29 in October, according to the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index.
October's reading marks the lowest homebuilder sentiment the US has seen since June 2012, the NAHB said, when the housing market was still moving through the aftermath of the 2008 crisis. It shows just how much builders have soured on the housing landscape amid rising costs and a record-breaking slowdown in home sales.
Here's what explains the decline:
"Housing remains squeezed by supply-side constraints and significant affordability challenges," Robert Dietz, the chief economist at the NAHB, said in a statement.

Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
The Housing Market Index remains well-below the midway threshold of 50, which suggests that homebuilding is solidly in contractional territory.
Most housing economists don't expect the outlook for sales or affordability to improve meaningfully anytime soon. That's largely because rates are likely to stay higher-for-longer, which will continue to act as a barrier for prospective buyers.
Sara Godfrey, an economist at Oxford Economics, said the latest "depressed" homebuilder sentiment reading was consistent with the firm's view that the housing market would remain stagnant all throughout next year.
Goldman Sachs also said it expects demand to remain "tepid," adding that existing home sales were likely to fall over the next several months.
Oliver Allen, a senior US economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, forecast a "meaningful slowdown" in new home sales, pointing to the impact of the recent surge in rates.
"If anything—confidence is likely to fall much further over the next month or two, given the recent trends in rates," he wrote in a client note on Monday.

articles.title_orig: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.title_zh: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.content_orig:
Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.
The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.
Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.
But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.
Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.
In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.
It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.
The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.
Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.
He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.
Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.
While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.
Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.
In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad.
"My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.
It is still not known when he might return to Spain.
Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.
The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.
The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.
But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.
The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.
But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.
And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

A Chinese-speaking hacker has been observed using artificial intelligence (AI) agents to probe and then gain unauthorized access to more than 100 websites belonging to some extremely well-known companies. From Deere, the farming equipment manufacturer, to SharkNinja, the company behind beloved kitchen appliances, the agents were able to leverage exposed instances of Carin, an open-source AI-powered problem-solving platform that has proven popular among hackers, a Reuters report explains.
This is just the latest example of hackers turning to AI agents in an attempt to level up their attacks on unsuspecting companies and services. Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge, spotted the hacker's antics when observing Carin instances that had been inadvertently exposed.
Fagerland was able to watch multiple hackers go about their business, but the Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific, the report says. They targeted businesses based in the United States, Canada, Australia, and Japanese e-commerce sites. Notably, the hacker didn't get into detail when commanding their legion of AI agents. Fewer than 100 Chinese characters were used, yet the agents had attempted ot break into more than 1,200 different websites as of the week ending October 18, 2026.
These agents weren't simply throwing everything at a wall and hoping it stuck, either. Security researcher Fagerland was "impressed" by some of the tactics that had been used. In one case, the AI agents scoured digital records to find infrastructure associated with their target, located a public-facing control panel, identified a weakness, and then leveraged it to force the execution of malicious commands, the Reuters report detailed. "It's ⁠not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland told Reuters . "It's not script kiddie stuff."
Vitally, the approach of using AI agents in this way means that they can be given instructions and then left to their own devices. With no supervision required, those commanding the agents are free to turn their attention elsewhere. While SharkNinja told Reuters that the attack only impacted a site used for product support information, the rest of the AI-aided hackers had more luck. One of the hackers monitored by Gargerland stole credit card data, while another tried to steal from a cryptocurrency exchange — although it isn't clear whether they were successful.

articles.title_orig: Violent protests multiply across Europe
articles.title_zh: Violent protests multiply across Europe
articles.content_orig:
School conditions, unaffordable housing and the cost of living have brought demonstrators on to the streets in several countries
Europe live – latest updates
Young people have been taking to the streets across Europe, including in Spain, France and Portugal , to protest over their unhappiness at the state of schools and the wider cost of living crisis.
In France, high school pupils have clashed with police in often violent protests over long hours, missing teachers, dilapidated classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. Pupils routinely miss months of teaching due to unfilled staff absences.
Other demonstrators soon joined in, voicing their unhappiness about rising living costs, including over fuel prices after US bombing in effect caused the closure of the strait of Hormuz. The General Confederation of Labour, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the protests and called for lower prices, higher pensions and boosted wages.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron , is nearing the end of his time in the Élysée Palace after serving two terms.
Over the Pyrenees in Spain , activists took to the streets in September over housing prices.
The protests were triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after an investment fund hiked her rent by 230%. Maricarmen Abascal died a fortnight later after being admitted to hospital.
Protesters have called for rent freezes, halting the evictions of vulnerable people and the regulation of short-term and room rentals.
Similar pleas were made across the Iberian border in Portugal on Saturday, when hundreds gathered in central Lisbon . Portuguese housing prices more than doubled between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice as fast as the EU average, according to official data.
Squeezed household budgets were also at the centre of marches in Milan. Masked rioters seemingly later seized on the protests to throw stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and setting fire to barricades made from bar tables. There were also clashes between police and protesters in Turin and Bologna.
Meanwhile, protests in Albania against the prime minister, Edi Rama, entered their seventh day on Monday. Demonstrators have said they are unhappy with perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.
The education protests in France began in late September, a week after the start of the school year. Protests soon also began springing up in Portugal and Belgium.
In France, demonstrations reached a high point on Saturday as about half a million people turned out to protest against the surging cost of living and join the students demanding better conditions at their schools. That day there were also marches in Belgium, Portugal and Italy.
In Albania, protests have been taking place since the summer, triggered by a luxury coastal development backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
In France, the government has said it will deploy 3,000 more substitute teachers to deal with shortages, and include students in decision-making for schools. It also scrapped plans to increase some university registration fees, which it had announced for next year’s budget.
Fuel protests in mid-September led to an announcement by the Élysée that the government would increase petrol subsidies for certain industries.
Spain’s Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, attempted to pass emergency housing legislation that included a ban on evictions until 2030 and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
The legislation’s defeat at the hands of rightwing and far-right parties in parliament led Sánchez to call a snap election for 29 November, as he told the public he needed a “broader progressive majority” to get new reforms through.
In recent days, the protests have been eclipsed by the violence that played out on the fringes. On Sunday night Macron said it was “unbearable to see our streets ransacked” while, hours later, France’s prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called for “very limited” and “localised” curfews.
Macron said a distinction must be drawn between what he described as genuine, peaceful demonstrators who were making demands over the cost of living and the education system, and others who “destroy, ransack and loot”.
His interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, appeared to signal the French government was not willing to concede further, as he blamed “far-left” protesters and “criminals who looted and ransacked” buildings across France. The country will go to the polls in April 2027.
Meanwhile, the protests continue. In Paris, about a dozen demonstrators blocked the entrance to the Louvre on Monday, leaving tourists milling outside the world’s most-visited museum.
In Spain, housing campaigners have vowed to keep up the pressure on politicians to address soaring costs, announcing plans for a general strike on 11 November.

articles.title_orig: F5 releases out-of-band patches for critical NGINX vulnerabilities
articles.title_zh: F5 releases out-of-band patches for critical NGINX vulnerabilities
articles.content_orig:
F5 has released out-of-band security patches to address multiple NGINX web server flaws, including three critical-severity vulnerabilities that can let attackers execute code on vulnerable systems.
The three critical vulnerabilities were found in the ngx_http_v3_module ( CVE-2026-15176 and CVE-2026-97205 ) and the NGINX map directive ( CVE-2026-93479 ).
Remote attackers without privileges can exploit them to launch denial-of-service (DoS) attacks or gain code execution on NGINX systems with non-default configurations.
Successful exploitation causes a heap-based buffer overflow or use-after-free in the NGINX worker process, leading to crashes or a restart. However, attackers may also be able to "execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR."
F5 released security patches for multiple NGINX software products affected by these two vulnerabilities, including NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source, NGINX Ingress Controller, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Instance Manager.
Security teams and admins who can't immediately install these security patches can mitigate CVE-2026-15176 by not using the 'alias' directive in a location block or the $request_filename variable, and CVE-2026-97205 by disabling asynchronous file I/O (AIO) or Server Side Includes (SSI).
CVE-2026-93479 can also be mitigated by using named captures instead of unnamed captures and limiting their use to the block with the regex match.
While F5 has not yet flagged these security issues as exploited in the wild, cybercrime and nation-state threat groups have often exploited vulnerabilities in F5 products in recent years.
For instance, attackers have targeted F5 security flaws to breach corporate networks , map internal servers , hijack devices , deploy data-wiping malware , and steal sensitive documents from victims worldwide.
Since November 2021, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged eight F5 vulnerabilities as actively exploited, four of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.
One year ago, in October 2025, F5 also disclosed that state-sponsored threat actors breached its systems in August 2025 and stole source code and information on undisclosed BIG-IP security vulnerabilities.
F5 is a Fortune 500 tech company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to over 23,000 customers, including 80% of the Fortune Global 500 and 48 Fortune 50 companies.
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court rejects alleged 9/11 mastermind’s attempt to revive plea deal
articles.content_orig:
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday rebuffed a bid from accused Sept. 11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices to revive plea agreements that they reached with military prosecutors before being revoked by the Biden administration.
In an unsigned order, the high court turned away the appeals from Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash of a lower court decision that prevented a military judge from enforcing pretrial agreements they reached with military prosecutors in 2024, which were withdrawn by then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.
In rejecting their case, the government's withdrawal of the plea deals remains in place. Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate in the court's consideration of the appeal.
Mohammed, Hawsawi and bin 'Atash, were captured in 2003 and charged before a military commission with several crimes for their alleged roles in crafting and perpetrating the Sept. 11 attacks, five of which carry the death penalty. In August, the judge overseeing their cases set a trial date of June 2028, which depends on the parties meeting certain deadlines and milestones on time.
The prosecutions have been mired in lengthy legal delays over whether evidence extracted during their interrogations could be used in court. The defendants were held at secret CIA prisons, where they were subjected to "enhanced interrogation techniques," or torture, before they were moved to Guantanamo Bay in 2006. They were formally charged in 2008.
In 2023, following the appointment of retired Brigadier General Susan Escallier as the Convening Authority for military commissions, military lawyers began discussing plea deals with the defendants. Agreements were subsequently reached in 2024 and approved by Escallier, who oversees the military court at Guantanamo Bay.
Under the terms of the deals, the defendants would plead guilty to all charges arising from their alleged roles in the 9/11 terror attacks and serve life sentences, avoiding the death penalty. But shortly after the agreements were announced, Austin said he was revoking them .
But a military judge ruled in November 2024 that Austin's nullification of the deals was unlawful, rendering the agreements valid and enforceable. A military appeals court then said Austin couldn't rescind the plea deals because the defendants had begun to perform one of the terms.
The Justice Department then asked the D.C. Circuit to step in and find that Austin validly withdrew from the pretrial agreements. The D.C. Circuit sided with the government in a decision last year and ruled that the defense secretary "indisputably" had the authority to withdraw from the plea deals.
"The Secretary acted within the bounds of his legal authority, and we decline to second-guess his judgment," the D.C. Circuit panel found.

articles.title_orig: Roche returns to China’s Hansoh for $15B biobucks ADC pact
articles.title_zh: Roche returns to China’s Hansoh for $15B biobucks ADC pact
articles.content_orig:
A year after their first antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) team-up, Roche has returned to Hansoh Pharmaceutical for a mammoth $15 billion biobucks pact.
The latest agreement spans a “broad portfolio of ADC programs,” Hansoh explained in an Oct. 19 release. They include two ADCs already in preclinical development at the Chinese biopharma, along with multiple programs focused on targets suggested by Roche but powered by Hansoh’s ADC tech.
The plan is for Jiangsu-based Hansoh to take these programs through phase 1 trials, before passing over responsibility to Roche to develop the ADCs worldwide—excluding Greater China.
In return, Hansoh will receive $400 million in upfront cash, followed by $110 million on the first anniversary of the deal. Further down the line, the biopharma is in line for potentially up to $15 billion in development, regulatory and commercialization milestones, as well as tiered royalties on sales if any ADCs make it to market.
The deal also has a clause where Hansoh could opt to contribute toward the global development of two programs from the collaboration. If it picks this route, Hansoh would become eligible to receive “incremental upside from the commercialization of these two programs,” according to the release.
This morning’s deal comes a year after Roche handed $80 million to Hansoh and pledged $1.45 billion in biobucks for the ex-China license to a CDH17-targeted ADC, dubbed HS-20110. At the time, HS-20110 was already in phase 1 testing in China and the U.S. as a potential treatment for colorectal cancer and other solid tumors.
“Building on the ADC partnership we announced last year, we are delighted to further strengthen our collaboration with Roche,” Eliza Sun, Executive Director of Hansoh’s board, said in this morning’s release.
“This new agreement reflects our shared commitment to advancing ADC innovation and underscores our strategy of leveraging our deep expertise to accelerate the development of transformative therapies for cancer patients globally,” Sun added.
Boris Zaïtra, head of corporate business development at Roche, said in this morning’s release that“expanding our strategic collaboration with Hansoh marks an important step in advancing our ADC vision.”
“Exploring next-generation ADCs is one of the most compelling frontiers in oncology today, offering the opportunity to address critical unmet needs and accelerate potential therapies for patients worldwide,” Zaïtra added.
Roche isn’t the only Big Pharma that’s turned to Hansoh to help power its ADC ambitions. GSK has already tasted clinical success with a pair of ADCs aimed at B7-H3 and B7-H4, respectively.
The B7-H3-directed ADC, dubbed ris-rez, recently achieved a median overall survival of 18.5 months in a phase 3 trial, lining up the therapy as a potential threat to Amgen and Merck & Co. in the lung cancer field. Last night, GSK unveiled the first global data for ris-rez, which demonstrated a 61% overall response rate in a phase 1b trial.
Jefferies analysts said that the readout helped move ris-rez from a therapy defined by its “impressive China phase 3” data to “a much more globally validated asset story.” Ris-rez is “starting to look like the B7-H3 ADC to beat in relapsed SCLC,” the analysts concluded.
Hong Kong-listed Hansoh has been one of the leading lights in China’s emergence as a biopharma innovation engine, notching collaborations with the likes of Merck & Co. and Regeneron . In August, Hansoh offered a bullish assessment of China’s innovative biopharma sector, arguing (PDF) that the industry is “fully transitioning from the ‘follower’ phase to the ‘frontrunner’ phase.”
This year, Hansoh stepped up spending to support its pipeline of more than 40 innovative medicine candidates that it is assessing in more than 70 clinical trials. R&D spending at the company jumped 20.7% to 1.7 billion Chinese yuan ($253 million) over the first half of the year.

articles.title_orig: California woman indicted on charges of spying for China targeting Taiwanese President's son (with video)
articles.title_zh: California woman indicted on charges of spying for China targeting Taiwanese President's son (with video)
articles.content_orig:
A California woman who prosecutors allege was spying on a son of Taiwan’s president was indicted this month on charges of conspiracy and being an unregistered foreign agent for China.
The indictment was filed Oct. 9 in U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, and the allegations it lays out mirror an earlier criminal complaint against the woman, Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine.
Prosecutors say Zhang, who also goes by Heather, spied on a son of Taiwan’s president outside his home in the Seattle area at the behest of Chinese officials. The spying is alleged to have taken place between roughly June and September 2025, prosecutors claim.
Taiwan is a self-ruled democracy that is the source of 90% of the world’s “leading-edge chip manufacturing,” according to the U.S. International Trade Administration . China claims Taiwan, which the U.S. has no official relationship with , though it is required by law to ensure Taiwan can defend itself.
Prosecutors allege Zhang was under the direction of an unnamed Chinese government official and former classmate at her alma mater, China’s University of International Relations, which is “closely affiliated with China’s intelligence apparatus,” an FBI investigator said in earlier court documents.
An example of the alleged activity was a request by the former classmate to send him pictures “of the house” where the son lives, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors alleged that Zhang flew from California to Las Vegas and then to the Seattle area to conduct surveillance of the unidentified son and his home from outside.
The indictment alleges she captured photos, video and license plate information and sent them to the person alleged to be her Chinese handler. An unidentified person, who had fled to China in September, was with her, prosecutors said.
Zhang also traveled to China in August 2025 to meet with a Chinese government official, returned days later and told the official she would most likely be going to where the victim was the following week, according to the indictment.
Her lawyer, Craig Harbaugh, did not immediately respond to a request for comment Sunday.
Previously, Harbaugh, a veteran criminal defense attorney, described Zhang as an upstanding resident of Irvine, about 42 miles southeast of Los Angeles, where she lives with her husband and two young daughters.
“The government’s theory — she’s been a sleeper agent for the last 10 years, working as a real estate agent, raising her family and will choose to go to China and abandon her work, her family and her home — it’s not supported,” Harbaugh said in court Oct. 7.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment late Sunday.
Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for the Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry, said this month after Zhang was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport that he was “not familiar” with the situation and that Beijing “opposes vilifying China by peddling the so-called ‘Chinese spy’ narrative.”
U.S. Magistrate Judge Steve Kim ordered Zhang held in pretrial detention after prosecutors argued she poses a flight risk. The U.S. Bureau of Prisons website shows that she remains in custody.
Zhang is scheduled to appear in federal district court Friday for a post-indictment arraignment. She could face up to 15 years in prison.
David Douglas is a supervising producer for NBC News based in Los Angeles.
Dennis Romero is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

Streaming video giant Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX) will be reporting earnings this Tuesday after market close. Here's what to look for.
Netflix met analysts' revenue expectations last quarter, reporting revenues of $12.56 billion, up 13.4% year on year. It was a softer quarter for the company, with EPS guidance for next quarter missing analysts' expectations and full-year revenue guidance meeting analysts' expectations.
Is Netflix a buy or sell going into earnings? Read our full analysis here, it's free for active Edge members .
This quarter, the market is expecting Netflix's revenue to grow 11.8% year on year, slowing from the 17.2% increase it recorded in the same quarter last year.
Analysts covering the company have generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days, suggesting they anticipate the business will stay the course heading into earnings. Netflix has missed Wall Street's revenue estimates multiple times over the last two years.
With Netflix being the first among its peers to report earnings this season, we don't have anywhere else to look to get a hint at how this quarter will unfold for consumer internet stocks. However, investors in the segment have had steady hands going into earnings, with share prices flat over the last month. Netflix is down 4.1% during the same time .
